lesson.title: Why Slot Machines Beat Paychecks at Keeping You Hooked
lesson.summary: Reinforcement can arrive on different schedules of timing and predictability, and the schedule itself, not just the reward, determines how fast a behavior is learned and how hard it is to extinguish.
lesson.body:
Positive and negative reinforcement both explain how consequences strengthen behavior, but neither one, on its own, says anything about how often or how predictably that reinforcement has to happen. B.F. Skinner's research showed that the pattern, or schedule, by which reinforcement is delivered changes everything about how a behavior is learned, how steadily it is performed, and how stubbornly it survives once the reinforcement stops.

The first big distinction is continuous versus partial reinforcement. Continuous reinforcement, rewarding every single correct response, produces fast learning but is also fragile: stop the rewards and the behavior fades quickly, since the organism notices the change almost immediately. Partial, or intermittent, reinforcement, rewarding only some responses, takes longer to establish the behavior in the first place, but the resulting behavior is far more resistant to extinction. This is called the partial reinforcement effect, and it explains a lot of stubborn habits.

Within partial reinforcement, schedules vary along two dimensions: whether reinforcement depends on the number of responses (ratio) or the amount of time that has passed (interval), and whether that number or time is fixed or variable.

A fixed-ratio (FR) schedule reinforces behavior after a set number of responses, like a coffee shop punch card that rewards a free drink after every ten purchases, or a factory worker paid per unit assembled. This produces a high, steady rate of responding with a brief pause right after each reinforcement, since the organism knows exactly how far away the next reward is. A variable-ratio (VR) schedule reinforces behavior after an unpredictable number of responses that averages out to some value, the way a slot machine pays out after a random number of pulls. Because you never know which response will be the one that pays off, variable-ratio schedules produce the highest, steadiest response rates of all, with almost no pause, and they are the most resistant to extinction of any schedule. This is exactly why gambling is so hard to walk away from: there is always a nagging sense that the very next pull might be the one.

Interval schedules work on time instead of count. A fixed-interval (FI) schedule reinforces the first response that occurs after a set amount of time has passed, like checking a slow-cooking oven or studying hardest right before a quiz that always happens on the same day each week. This produces a distinctive scalloped pattern: responding drops right after reinforcement and climbs as the deadline approaches. A variable-interval (VI) schedule reinforces the first response after an unpredictable amount of time, like refreshing your phone for a text that could arrive at any moment, or a pop quiz that could happen on any day. Because you can never predict exactly when the payoff window will open, VI schedules produce a slow, steady rate of responding without the scallop. A teacher who wants consistently prepared students, rather than students who cram right before a predictable test, is essentially choosing a variable schedule over a fixed one.
